claims.text: The system is a CoCrFeMnNi HEA coating deposited on a transition-metal matrix such as steel.
CoCrFeMnNi has a metastable fcc structure under the initial conditions.
CoCrFeMnNi has a low stacking-fault energy of approximately 20 mJ m−2.
Low stacking-fault energy facilitates the fcc-to-hcp transformation through stacking faults, dislocations, and twinning.
In CoCrFeMnNi, hcp is thermodynamically favored at lower temperatures and higher pressures, whereas fcc is favored at higher temperatures and lower pressures.
The tribologically induced hcp phase fraction mediates the effect of ambient temperature on wear resistance.
At low temperature, fcc CoCrFeMnNi can remain kinetically trapped despite the lower-temperature thermodynamic preference for hcp.
Tribological stress induces a sluggish and irreversible fcc-to-hcp transformation in the coating.
Low-temperature stress-induced hcp formation causes work hardening and improves wear resistance.
Increasing temperature lowers the kinetic barrier for the fcc-to-hcp transition.
Increasing temperature through approximately 600 °C stabilizes fcc and suppresses hcp formation.
Above approximately 800 °C, thermal activation makes rapid fcc-to-hcp nucleation kinetically accessible under tribological stress.
Rapid high-temperature hcp formation causes phase instability and loss of ductility.
Brittle fracture of hcp regions accelerates abrasive wear.
Wear rate decreases between 25 °C and approximately 600 °C.
Wear rate increases sharply above approximately 800 °C.
Approximately 800 °C is the critical degradation boundary for the coating under tribological stress.
The critical temperature depends on alloy composition, coating thickness, and sliding conditions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats suppression of brittle hcp as the reason heating to about 600 °C improves wear resistance, while the mechanism says low-temperature hcp formation produces work hardening and improved wear resistance. The opposite effects assigned to hcp formation are not reconciled.

The structural mediator states that higher temperature favors fcc over hcp, but the proposed boundary attributes degradation above about 800 °C to thermally enabled fcc-to-hcp transformation. A kinetic explanation is asserted, but no rationale is given for why it reverses the stated high-temperature phase preference.
